title: KDDI Plans Drone Deliveries for Lawson Products
paragraphs: Japanese telecommunications company KDDI is planning to use drones to deliver products from Lawson, one of Japan's largest convenience store chains, to customers' homes.

On October 27, 2026, KDDI and its subsidiary KDDI SmartDrone signed a partnership with Wing, a drone delivery company owned by Google's parent company, Alphabet. The companies aim to start delivering goods by drone in a few selected areas of Japan by the end of 2027. The deliveries are expected to include food, daily necessities, medicines that can be bought without a prescription and small orders from shops.

Under the partnership, Wing will provide the drones, the software used to control flights and automated equipment on the ground. Meanwhile, KDDI will provide the communications network and handle regulations and cooperation with local governments. KDDI SmartDrone controls drones through KDDI's mobile network, which allows them to fly beyond the sight of the people controlling them.

Lawson is the only retailer that has been named so far. KDDI and the trading company Mitsubishi each own half of Lawson. The two companies have already worked together on drone deliveries. For example, in February 2025, Lawson and KDDI SmartDrone tested delivering fried chicken snacks and packages by drone in Chichibu, in Saitama Prefecture.

The companies believe drone delivery could help solve several problems in Japan. According to an estimate by Japan's agriculture ministry in 2020, about 9 million people have difficulty getting to food stores. Japan is also facing a shortage of truck drivers. In addition, drones could be useful during disasters, when roads are blocked.
Wing has completed more than one million home deliveries, mainly in the United States. Japan will be the first new country for the company since Ireland.

However, drone delivery is still expensive. A Lawson executive said that a single drone round trip could cost several thousand yen, so it is not yet something customers can use casually. In addition, Japan's rules for drone delivery are still developing, so getting permission may take time.
